Suggested Commonwealth Conference (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 28, 1950. Perhaps I might be permitted to put the two amendments on the record at this point. The amendment moved this afternoon by the leader of the opposition asks that the usual words be deleted and that the following words be substituted:
this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
The other amendment to a motion to go into supply to which I have already referred, which was made on February 28, 1950, by the hon. member for Lake Centre, is found at page 308 of Hansard for that year. After the usual introductory words it reads as follows:
this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets, and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.
Hon. members will notice that the two amendments are much the same. The only difference of note is that in the amendment moved this afternoon the leader of the opposition has made reference to that difficult problem, the convertibility of commonwealth currencies. When the amendment was moved on February 28, 1950, some three members of this group-our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy)-spoke on the amendment and indicated that we were prepared to support it. It was made clear on that occasion, however, that we were prepared to support the amendment on the understanding that it did not purport to establish a restrictive type of trade within the countries of the commonwealth alone. We felt that the proposal asked for every effort to be made to increase trade within the countries of the commonwealth, without detracting from trade between Canada and other nations of the world. Indeed it is our feeling that if we can increase trade among the commonwealth nations we will be doing a service not only to Canada and the other nations of the commonwealth; we will be doing a service to the entire world. We will help to stimulate world trade and to bring to all the nations of the world the advantages that flow from trade.

Suggested Commonwealth Conference
It is because the amendment that has been moved this afternoon, while it asks for a conference of commonwealth nations to discuss trade within the commonwealth, does not restrict trade to commonwealth nations, that we are prepared to support the amendment now before the house.
When we look at this whole question of trade it is desirable that we ask ourselves some simple and fundamental questions. Why is trade important? Why are we so anxious to increase the flow of trade throughout the world? The leader of the opposition (Mr. (Drew) emphasized its importance to the prosperity of our various nations. He also emphasized its relationship to our defence effort. We agree. But he also had a good deal to say about the desirability of freeing trade so that individual men and women might pursue their individual initiative and vigour in the custom and manner of days gone by. With that aim we disagree. We do not think of trade quite in those terms; we do not think of it as an activity to be left to the exploitation of individual traders. We believe that trade between nations, like the division of labour within a community, adds to the economic wealth of the nations that participate in that trade. Trade adds to the economic wealth of the world, and it is for that reason that we feel every possible step should be taken to increase our trade with the other nations of the commonwealth, and indeed with all the nations of the world. To do this means not less activity by governments, but an even greater effort on their part.
Let us not forget the simple rules about foreign trade that most of us probably learned when we studied the rudiments of economics. We know that even though we may be able to produce each of a number of products cheaper than some other country can produce those same products, nevertheless it is to our mutual advantage to produce for trading those products in connection with which we have the relatively greatest advantage. It is a proposition that can be demonstrated not only in theoretical terms; it has certainly been demonstrated in practice, and it does behoove us to pursue the policy of the widest possible trade.
I said a moment ago that we are concerned for expanded trade not to provide a field for exploitation by individuals. We are anxious to have the greatest possible flow of trade so that the people of our country, the people of other countries whose economies at the moment might be on a par with ours, and in due course the people of underdeveloped countries might enjoy the higher standard of living which is possible by applying labour power to the resources the world

possesses at the present time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we feel that any move that can be taken to facilitate trade, even a conference to discuss ways and means of increasing it among a selected group of countries, is all to the good; and we do not like to see the government turn down a suggestion of that kind.
The last words of the former debate to which I have already referred, namely, the one which took place on February 28, 1950 on the same subject, were spoken by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), when he said, as recorded in Hansard of that year at page 337:
Whether or not a conference of this kind would accomplish anything, surely it would be an advance if we could bring the nations of the commonwealth close together-the commonwealth now is both east and west-and find out more definitely what each nation has to sell and what each is willing to buy. Surely if we did not do anything more than make an advance in that direction, the conference would be worth while. Unless those who are opposed to such a conference have some better solution for meeting our economic problems, they certainly should not turn this one down without giving a serious consideration indeed.
It is in those terms, Mr. Speaker, that we feel this motion should be considered. We recognize that it should go further. We recognize that our concern is for trade amongst all the nations of the world, not just some of them; but here is a step in the right direction. Here is a move, the aim of which is to increase the trading that takes place and thereby to help to raise living standards, and we feel that it should be supported.
We made it clear on the occasion of the previous debate that we did not agree with any of the restrictive measures that might seem to be implied in a conference of commonwealth nations only. If the leader of the opposition had indicated that this was a request for the calling of the kind of conference that met in this city in 1932, our attitude toward it would be different. But so long as the purpose of this conference is to expand trade, to take positive measures in that direction, as I have already indicated we are prepared to give it our support.
Now, Mr. Speaker, discussing this whole question of trade and its importance to the whole world, I feel that perhaps I can do no better at this point than quote part of what my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East had to say on this question when the subject was debated on the previous occasion to which I have already referred. At page 336 of Hansard for 1950 he said:
In my view this would not necessarily be a serious matter were it not for the fact that, as I see it, the present deterioration in trade and in world economic conditions follows a pattern we know so well. That was the pattern after the last war, when we had a few short years of economic activity when we were urged by businessmen to produce

more and consume less. But shortly came the debacle, when a great many people could not consume at all, not because the things were not there to consume but because something had gone wrong with the exchange of commodities both between nations and within the nation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East went on to say:
At the present time we see the very same pattern developing. When we finished the war we had a tremendous backlog of needs to be met, both in consumer and capital goods. This was more so with the countries of Europe than on this continent of North America, but in four or five short years we have overcome that backlog of consumer needs, we have added to our capital resources so that now we can supply a greater amount of goods and services than ever before. Now, the paradox of the situation is this: just when we are better equipped than ever before to supply the needs of our people and raise the standard of living, the standard of living is going down.
Hon. members are aware that this is true. Despite the larger number of dollars people may have in their pockets, and despite the greater volume of production of which Canada now boasts in terms of our gross national product, the fact of the matter is that the value of those dollars has so decreased that we are not maintaining the health and living standards of our people. I wish to quote a bit further from the observations of my colleague:
How far that deterioration may go on this particular lap I do not know; but if we do not find some way to distribute the wealth we can produce so abundantly, nothing can save us from falling into a depression such as we had from 1930 to 1939, from which we were rescued by the war.
That is the paradox of our time. We find ourselves confronted in the world of the fifties with capacity to produce simply undreamed of. Yet at this very time, when we have it within our power as a civilization to produce a standard of living that would be a blessing to mankind the world over, instead of moving toward that condition we find ourselves on the brink of disaster of one kind or another. The fear of war, or the fear of economic collapse, is with us daily.
Surely the direction that we should take in an effort to resolve that paradox is to aim at the greatest possible production of goods and services, and at the widest possible distribution of those goods and services, not only within a nation such as our own but among all peoples the world over. It has been put this afternoon in economic terms by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), that this whole question of trade is a two-way street. That is a truism often repeated; and how true it is, that we cannot expect people to buy the goods we produce unless we are prepared to buy goods from them.

We of this group see it not only in its economic terms but in human terms, in terms of human progress, in terms of the survival of our civilization. We feel that unless we can find ways not only to produce an abundance of goods but also to distribute those goods where they are needed, our civilization stands in imminent danger. That effort to distribute, as I have already said, must be carried out on two fronts. It must be carried on among our own people and it must be carried on across the world. Indeed, it is our responsibility to make for the widest possible distribution of the surplus wealth we can produce on this North American continent, and to distribute it among the backward and undeveloped nations of the world.
The leader of the opposition this afternoon said, and rightly, that this whole question of trade among the nations of the commonwealth, and among western nations generally, is vital to our defence. We agree; but we would emphasize the fact that it is not only a matter of supplying each other mutually with the arms and weapons of defence in a military sense, but it is even more important to our defence that by production of an abundance of goods and services, by distribution and by trade we improve the prosperity and well-being of all our own peoples in the western nations, and that we do everything possible to improve the well-being and the standard of living of peoples in other parts of the world.
We are conscious of the fact that we are up against a stubborn enemy today. That enemy is using two weapons. He is using the weapons of war, and he is also using the weapon of an idea. That idea, to some of the people to whom it is being sold, may be an illusion. But the enemy is using the weapon of that idea, for he claims that he knows a way of enabling people who are now hungry to get food, and people who are now in poverty to enjoy a higher standard of living.
Even if the idea he is using as his chief weapon is an illusion, the fact remains that it is making headway; and one of the reasons it is making headway is that we are not using it sufficiently ourselves. I submit it is our task in the present world situation to make use of both weapons ourselves; and we are in a position to do so-and to do so to so much greater advantage.
I need not spend time on the fact that we are in a position to develop the military side of our defence program. We are doing that; indeed we may be overdoing it. But what about that other weapon, the weapon of the idea that people do not have to live in perpetual hunger, want and poverty, whether

Suggested Commonwealth Conference they are in the great industrial cities of North America or in the backward countries of south and southeast Asia. I submit it is our task to develop our ideas about trade, not only in terms of the prosperity that can come to us by freer trade but also in terms of what we can do to sell a better idea than the enemy is trying to sell to the backward, starving and impoverished peoples in large areas of the world.
It was this sort of idea I had in mind when in my opening remarks I indicated that in my view the subject that has been opened up this afternoon transcends in importance the precise terms of the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and transcends the importance of doing what we can-desirable and important as that may be-to improve the prosperity and well-being of our own land and those other nations associated with us in the commonwealth.
I have already taken the liberty of quoting at some length from a speech by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, on February 28, 1950. I should like to quote further from what he said on that occasion, as it is reported at page 337 of Hansard for that year:
In my opinion, it is not just a question of improving Canada's trade position, it is a question of international prosperity-the prosperity of the countries of the western world. But it is more than that; it is as much a part of our defence against aggression as is our military preparedness. If we do not keep the western world prosperous, we will lose out in the struggle with the totalitarian world. Let us remember that to maintain the prosperity of the western world is part of our defence against aggression. It is for that reason this question is so important. That is why increasing unemployment and falling markets are so important to everyone who believes in co-operation and peace.
May I interject to suggest that it does not matter where people are feeling the pinch of falling markets, or where people are suffering from unemployment; whether it be in North America, Europe, Asia, or wherever it may be, it is a matter of importance not only to them, but likewise to those of us in Canada and to the peoples of the whole world. I quote further:
We also must not forget that we cannot have cooperation in military matters to defend ourselves against an enemy, and have trade wars between the co-operators. Surely the time has arrived when we should see that that sort of economics no longer fits the needs of the world of 1950.
What was said on that occasion as applying to the world of 1950 applies with equal strength to the world of 1952. And so, Mr. Speaker, in what I have said I have attempted to indicate that while we would like to see something broader than what has been proposed by the leader of the opposition, so far as it goes it is a contribution. Anything that will make it possible for a group of nations

such as the nations of the commonwealth to sit down and discuss ways and means of expanding trade and improving their prosperity and well-being is a contribution not only to the people of Canada and the other nations of the commonwealth but also a contribution toward the prosperity and well-being of the whole world. It is a step toward progress. It leads away from poverty, suffering and starvation of which there is far too much amongst the peoples of the world, and toward that better standard of living which today we have it within our power to provide. Any step in that direction should be supported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to add to what my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has said in connection with this amendment. I think every hon. member in the house would be in agreement with the purposes of the amendment. We are all anxious to see the currencies of the trading nations of the world made fully convertible. We are all anxious to explore-I am using the language of the amendment-all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends. Like my colleague, if I thought that another conference would really advance either of those objectives I would heartily support the holding of such a conference.
As he pointed out, we are attending commonwealth conferences every year, sometimes several times a year, at which questions of trade and convertibility are discussed. The most recent one I attended was in London in January when a conference of finance ministers was held at which this and related questions were discussed at considerable length.
There are certain points we should bear in mind when we are discussing this question of the convertibility of currencies. I suppose I need not remind the house that the currency of one of the commonwealth countries, Canada, is and has been for over a year fully convertible. The currencies of all the other commonwealth countries, with the exception of South Africa, are based upon sterling; that is to say, the reserves of gold and foreign exchange are held by the Bank of England. When any of those countries earns dollars or other foreign currency as a result of its trading operations that currency is turned in to the Bank of England which gives it a sterling credit in exchange.
I think it is pretty well recognized that one of the requisites for the convertibility of any currency is that there should be adequate reserves of gold and convertible foreign exchange to back it up. I have not the

slightest doubt that the United Kingdom and the other commonwealth countries are just as anxious as anyone else to make sterling convertible. But they feel they cannot afford to take that risk until their reserve position is sufficiently strong to enable them to do so. When that can be done, of course, is a matter of judgment.
I have been going to commonwealth finance conferences for about six years, and have had the opportunity of discussing these matters with four chancellors of the exchequer. In every case I have pointed out that in Canada we did not believe that the continuation of discriminatory quantitative restrictions was the road to convertibility. I have pointed out that while we recognize that measures of this kind were no doubt necessary as a temporary expedient, they were no longer the appropriate cure in the long run and that the final solution for the convertibility of a country's currency lay in internal measures as well as external, and primarily in measures of internal policy.
That being the case, the time and the conditions under which the currencies of other commonwealth countries will become convertible will depend upoi} a decision to be taken primarily by the government of the United Kingdom which holds the reserves of gold and foreign exchange of those countries and which acts as banker for them. At the conference in January the question of convertibility was discussed, and it was laid down as a principle that the sterling area countries should work toward convertibility. Needless to say we most heartily endorsed that objective. We are only too ready to do what we can to facilitate it.
May I say in passing that for the past four or five years Canada has at least done her share toward achieving that end by making a contribution in the form of loans to countries in the sterling area of something in excess of a billion and a quarter dollars. Where the decision to be taken is essentially for the countries whose currencies are now unconvertible, under those circumstances it does seem to me that it would be quite inappropriate for Canada to initiate another conference following the series of conferences that have been held, at which we have been represented and at which we have endeavoured to make our views crystal clear. It would be quite inappropriate for Canada to suggest that a conference of commonwealth countries should be called to determine when and how the currencies of other members of the commonwealth should be made convertible.

It is for that reason and on that aspect of the amendment that I feel it would be quite improper for us to make such a suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a word on this amendment and I want to make it clear that the words I am going to say will apply only to the amendment. For that reason I want to put it on record. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends."
The reason I put that on the record is the fact that on other occasions this party has strongly stressed that some steps should be taken to make possible the convertibility of other currencies, particularly those of the sterling area, so our trade would not be hampered by the United Kingdom being short of United States or Canadian dollars. I well recall that not long ago when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was in England he made the statement-I speak only from memory but I think I am close to being correct-that dollars should not stand in the way of greater trade between Canada and the United Kingdom, particularly in view of the fact that Great Britain was so greatly in need of goods we can produce, when she desired them to the utmost and the only reason she could not get them was that she did not have the dollars.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) have pointed out that on many occasions they have attended conferences of one kind and another at which convertibility and trading matters were discussed, yet nothing material had developed. That indicates to me that it might be necessary to have a special conference called such as is indicated by the amendment to try to come to some conclusions whereby the convertibility of currencies might be achieved.
We are particularly in need of foreign markets for our agricultural products. It has been stressed on many occasions by members of this party and others that there is a great need for export markets for agricultural goods. Only a week or two ago Dr. E. C. Hope, one of the outstanding economists in this country, who is attached to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, made a statement that the net income of agriculture this year would be greatly reduced compared with

Suggested Commonwealth Conference 1950 and 1951 because of the falling off of our trade. Certainly everyone acquainted with agriculture can see quite readily that agricultural production is dropping, and it is not because we have not the facilities to increase production or because there is a shortage of actual markets. The people of these different countries are greatly in need of our agricultural production, and the only thing that stands in the way is the difficulty of paying us in dollars. In the past we have achieved wonderful successes in other lines, and it seems to me it should not be impossible for all the commonwealth countries, and others as well, to get together for the express purpose of ironing out the difficulty of convertibility of currencies. It should be possible to find some method.
In fact I will go so far as to say that when the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was speaking in the house not long ago on this very subject he gave the government some very good suggestions as to how they might go about it. Because the hon. member for Acadia has discussed this matter on many occasions, has advised the government on possible ways of doing it and has pointed out the necessity of having convertibility of currencies so those countries which are in need of our goods may obtain them, thus increasing Canadian production not only in agriculture but also in other lines, I think it is not necessary for me to go further into the matter at this time. I merely want to make it clear that in supporting this measure as we intend to do we are only supporting the amendment outlined by the leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment seeks to focus the attention of members of the house on a problem we believe is of great importance to Canada at the present time, namely the position of our trade with the other nations of the commonwealth. Your Honour will notice that it merely asks the government to consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and also to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.

submissions with respect to the amendment, and then having made his speech got up and left the chamber.

This question is particularly serious for the province of British Columbia. I propose to say a few words about the difficulties that people in certain occupations in that province are having by reason of the present situation in commonwealth trade. Before proceeding to point out those difficulties, I think it would be well for the members of the house to realize that there are certain basic facts in existence at the present time which cannot be talked away by either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Finance. They are in existence and they must be faced. The first is that the proportion of Canada's trade which is with the British commonwealth has been steadily falling. In 1938 our exports to commonwealth countries amounted to approximately 48 per cent of our total exports. Imports from commonwealth countries amounted to about 30 per cent of total imports. Last year we find that this trade had fallen until it was down to 20 per cent. The very fact that there has been this great decrease in the proportion of our trade with the commonwealth is sufficient to justify the calling of a conference such as is suggested by the amendment.
Another fact which must be borne in mind is that Canada is steadily becoming more dependent on the United States for both her export and import trade. I have here the annual report of the Department of Trade 55704-181

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I may meet the wishes of the hon. member for Fraser Valley and also the wishes of the chairman, I shall attempt to do so.

The amendments contained in this bill respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company are slight. The history of this company was somewhat checkered in that they had a serious accident in connection with the bridge several years ago. The then Vancouver harbour commissioners, now the national harbours board, took over the responsibility of the bridge under an agreement with the company; and included in that agreement was provision for the payment of a sum of $35,000 and an undertaking to repair the damage to the bridge resulting from an accident in connection with a ship. This involved the removal of a bascule span and the installation of a straight lift span at a cost of $1 million. It was part of the agreement that the bridge would be returned to the company-which is a public company, the shares all being owned by four municipalities that are served in the area- as soon as the sum of approximately $1,035,000 was discharged. That debt is now discharged and the bridge has been returned to the company which, as I say, is the four municipalities which it serves.
The first amendment amends section 7 of the act of incorporation, which provides that the directors of the company shall be the mayors or reeves of the four cities or municipalities concerned. The councils of those cities and municipalities are desirous that any member of the council may be appointed as a director rather than a requirement that it be the mayor or the reeve of the municipality. It would not be compulsory for the mayor or the reeve to sit. Under this amendment the mayor or the reeve could be appointed, but any other member of the council likewise could be appointed. That explains section 7.
Section 8 is amended to provide for clarification of the word "tolls". This is a bridge which has railway tracks in the centre and a roadway on each side. The company is desirous of entering into a twenty-one year agreement with the Canadian National Railways with respect to the use of the rails. They want to make certain that their authority in respect of the tolls on the roadway is absolutely clear, and that they have the authority to charge tolls for motor vehicles and even for pedestrians. That is why this provision is put in. There is also a provision which indicates that they will have power, under regulation, to enforce speed limits and so on on the roadways on the bridge. I think we can assume that the regulations they make will be in accordance with the provincial law respecting speed limits and that they undoubtedly will coincide with the bylaws of the municipalities concerned. I think it is entirely reasonable to suppose that this 55704-181 i

authority is being asked because, in all likelihood, the speed limit they will require on that bridge will be somewhat less than the provincial minimum speed limit.
The last amendment amends section 14, which has to do only with the correction of names. Some of the railway companies with which agreements will be reached, and involving wheelage by the Canadian National Railways across that bridge, were incorrectly named. All this section does is give those railways their correct names.

I am glad to support this bill because I think these four municipalities which own the company known as the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company deserve great credit for the enterprise they have shown in connection with the bridge.
The company was formed in 1910, and the bridge was built in the 1920's, I believe, at a time when there was no connecting bridge whatever across the harbour at Vancouver. The bridge at that time filled a great need. It has been of great importance in the development of what is known as the north shore, comprising the municipalities of the city of North Vancouver, the district of north Vancouver and the municipality of west Vancouver. In addition, it has helped greatly in the development of the city of Vancouver itself.
As the hon. member for Vancouver South has said, one of the spans of the bridge was knocked out some few years after the original erection. That resulted in a change in the type of bridge, and then the depression came along and eventually the government had to step in to help with the bridge. In recent years the indebtedness to the government has been paid off and the company, which

is owned by the municipalities, has taken the bridge back. They require the amendments contained in this bill in order to facilitate their business operations. Because of that fact I personally am very glad to support the measure.

I should like to say just a word in connection with this bill. I have no desire to take up any unnecessary time, and I agree with what my hon. friend for Vancouver South has said. I almost agree with what my friend the hon. member for Fort William has said, except he forgot to mention the head of the great lakes.
I had the privilege of representing the people concerned in this bill for several years when the original sponsor was serving in Sicily and Italy. I represented his riding, then known as Vancouver North and now Coast-Capilano. He is to be congratulated, and I think the temporary sponsor, the hon. member for Vancouver South, is to be congratulated for giving such a clear-cut story of the bill, in spite of the fact that it does not please my friend the hon. member for Fort William. I admit that it is difficult to satisfy him.
Perhaps some of you do not know the exact position this bridge occupies between the third city of Canada and the fast-growing fourth city of Canada. We have in Vancouver, Mr. Chairman, not only the third industrial city in Canada but the third in population. And joined up by this and another bridge we have what I might describe as the most scenic cities in the Dominion of Canada, West Vancouver and North Vancouver. I heard interjections from behind me that they are now eighth and ninth. I believe the interjection came from Nova Scotia. Then to my left I heard interjections from Toronto, which is a very fine city, Mr. Chairman, and will be following Vancouver for many years to come. But this bridge is to connect these two great cities, the one the great industrial and port city of the Pacific ocean and the outlet for the Dominion of Canada to the whole Pacific ocean and the great Asiatic market we have before us, and the cities of West Vancouver and North Vancouver.
There is another thing in connection with it, because railroads are brought into the picture. I notice that the names of certain railroads are mentioned in one of the paragraphs here. Some day the Pacific Great Eastern, through the efforts of my good friend from Cariboo, will be brought down and will connect the great port of Vancouver and North Vancouver, bringing down all the produce of that great district, northern British Columbia
IMr. Green.]
and northern Alberta, and making it available to the great market we have for the future in Asia.
I am sure the hon. member for Cariboo will have a few words to say in this connection. If we do not have this bridge there is no possible way that we can have a connection between the great cities of West and North Vancouver and Vancouver, Mr. Chairman, the third largest city in Canada, which will be the largest city in Canada within ten years.
I do not want to delay this legislation, but I do hope that in the absence of the original sponsor of this bill, who is serving us all at the United Nations in New York, we shall all see fit to support it.

Yes. This is a bill to incorporate an insurance company. The purpose is to take over the assets and liabilities and assume the rights and obligations of a provincial insurance company which was incorporated in the province of Quebec. The provincial company was incorporated in 1901 and has been carrying on business ever since as a fire insurance company.
Most of the clauses of the bill are to permit the company to operate as a mutual

Private Bills
insurance company. It will sell insurance both on a cash premium basis and on the mutual basis. The board of directors will be elected, one third by the mutual policyholders; the capital will be half a million dollars, and the amount of capital that is to be subscribed before the company can begin business will be $100,000.
Section 6 of the bill enumerates 26 kinds of insurance the company wishes to be authorized to sell. It will be covered by the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932. The main purpose of the company is the sale of fire insurance. At the meetings each shareholder will have one vote per share, and each policyholder will have one vote per $1,000 of insurance. This bill has passed the Senate and has been approved by the superintendent of insurance. I would ask that after second reading it be referred to the committee on banking and commerce.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, I feel greatly
honoured in being able to present this bill because the president and secretary of the Canadian dental association were both classmates of mine. It has taken them thirty years to finally evolve a program with respect to the standardization of certificates which is now universally accepted by every province in the Dominion of Canada. Before I pass on to a short explanation of the bill may I pay tribute to the hon. member for Queens-Shelburne (Mr. Smith) who had he been here in all probability would have presented this bill instead of myself. As we well know, misfortunes befall us all and I am sure I express the feeling of every hon. member in this house when I say how much we regret that the hon. member is not here to either present this bill or to assist in its presentation.
The object of the legislation is to make it possible for dental practitioners to establish by a single set of examinations that they possess the training and qualifications to meet the requirements of the dental licensing board of the province in which they desire to practise.
Provision is being made for the establishment of a national dental examining board which would establish standards, arrange for examination of candidates, issue certificates of qualification and maintain a register of qualified persons. Consideration has been given to the retention of the autonomy of the provincial licensing boards. Each province will have one member on the national board, the additional two members to make up a total membership of twelve being from the

Canadian dental association. Any province may withdraw from participation in the plan on twelve months' notice.
The board referred to In the bill will not issue licences; it will simply issue certificates of qualification which will be recognized by each participating province and the licensing board thereof. This plan is recommended by the Canadian dental association and has been evolved after consultation and negotiation with the licensing bodies of the provinces, which negotiations have extended over a period of years. The plan is analogous to that followed by the Canadian medical association with respect to medical practitioners. Chapter 129 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, sets up the medical council of Canada. The provisional members of the board are the president, the president-elect and the registrar-secretary of the Canadian dental association.
In conclusion I want to point out clearly and distinctly that the governing bodies in the different provinces have worked on this scheme for some thirty years and agreement has finally been reached with each province, including our newest province of Newfoundland. This legislation will not take away one iota of the authority of the provincial governing bodies or the Canadian dental association, but it does bring into being something that has been long desired by practising dental surgeons in this country. Having graduated they feel that they should be allowed, after having obtained a proper certificate of qualification, to practise in any province they may choose, which they cannot do at the present time. I would move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the bill now before us is the granting of a charter to another pipe line company, and I intend to support it. Other companies have made similar applications to the house, have appeared before the standing committee and have been granted charters. The granting of a charter to this company will simply allow them to proceed to do business. Whether or not the pipe line will be built will depend on a lot of other factors. I should also like to point out that I am in favour of the export of natural gas from the province of Alberta, but when I say that I believe there are certain conditions and reservations with respect to such export. That is where probably some hon. members of the Social Credit party, and also the hon. member for Calgary West, will differ with me.
There are two schools of thought in Alberta with regard to the export of natural gas. One school urges the rapid exploitation of our natural gas reserves for the purpose of making speculative profits now regardless of whether or not future long-range industrial requirements can be met. The other school of thought believes there should be export of natural gas if and when Alberta's future industrial needs are adequately provided for. It is simply an orderly long-range policy for the purpose of making the maximum use of

Alberta's natural resources at home by the development of industry.
If Canada is going to become a strong nation I believe every province must prosper and develop. Alberta is simply one of the three prairie provinces. We in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have tremendous natural resources, but one of the greatest resources of any country or province is its population. One of the things we are lacking today in the prairie provinces is population. Some sixty years ago Edward Blake lamented "an empty west, empty still". If you compare the 1901 census with the 1951 census you will note that fifty years after the opening and growth of the west it still has nowhere near enough population to sustain it. In fact the 1951 census shows that after a scant fifty years of growth the west has entered a period of decline, and when I refer to the west I mean the three prairie provinces.
Let us take the province of Alberta. In my opinion the census figures for 1951 do not portray a true picture of what has happened there. You will see that there is an increase in population of some 140,000, but a very important factor is not taken into account, namely the natural increase. By "natural increase" I mean the number of births over and above the number of deaths. If you were to take the 1941 population and add to it the natural increase, and if you did not allow anything for people coming into the province from other provinces or other countries, you would find that in the province of Alberta there has been a net loss of population in the last ten years of 9,500 people. The results for Saskatchewan and Manitoba are much more disastrous. You will note that in the three prairie provinces the net loss in population amounts to a quarter of a million people. In other words we have not only failed to attract people to the three prairie provinces; we have failed to keep people who were already there. The prairie provinces are essentially agricultural in nature. As an Albertan I say that what we want in Alberta are industries, and the same is true of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Already industries are coming in as a result of our natural gas. We want more industries coming into Alberta so our young men and women can find not only jobs but better opportunities in that province; so they will not have to go to the end of the pipe line seeking better opportunities.
I understand that in the province of Quebec during the last forty years people have been allowed to cut timber as long as it could be processed into pulp. The result has not only benefited the province of Quebec but it has been of great benefit to the whole dominion of Canada-somebody may want to say, "to the realm of Canada".

Some people like to compare Alberta with Texas. When you consider Alberta, it is my submission that it is hardly a fair comparison because my information is that before Texas agreed to export natural gas from that state they were assured that they had some 90 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. In Alberta, according to the figures we have-and there are various figures-we have only somewhere around four trillion cubic feet of natural gas. In other words it is not fair to compare Texas with Alberta, although we would like to be in the position of Texas.
Alberta can be compared to the state of Montana immediately south of us. I understand that some years ago the state of Montana started to export their natural gas. What has happened today? In order to sustain one of their industries, the Anaconda copper industry, they have had to beg for natural gas from the province of Alberta. They ran out of natural gas.
We believe, lacking other proof, that the fields of Montana are just a continuation of those in Alberta. In other words we do not want to be placed in the same position as that state. That is why I would much prefer an orderly, long-range policy, making the maximum use of our natural resources to strengthen Alberta and Canada as a whole, rather than acting as a voice for the speculator.
Mr. Chairman, if you noticed, the hon. member for Peace River has seen fit to pour a certain amount of abuse upon some individuals, me in particular, by referring to me as an adolescent. He made the same reference to the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta, and he made the same reference to the hon. member for Charlotte. I do not know whether I want to answer or follow the same method of argument. I think I will just leave him entirely alone, but I would like to make some reference to what has been said, or to at least why in my opinion most of the members of the Social Credit group in this house oppose this particular bill.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was speaking in support of the amendment which was moved by the leader of the apposition and which urged that the government take steps to convene a conference of the nations of the commonwealth for the purpose of seeking means by which there might be convertibility of commonwealth currencies and exploring the possibility of restoring and enlarging the traditional markets within that commonwealth. I had pointed out that in connection with our trade there are certain basic factors which must be kept in mind in a discussion of this sort, particularly the fact that the proportion of Canada's trade with the commonwealth has been steadily falling in recent years until it is now only 20 per cent of our total export trade. I had also pointed out that we are becoming steadily more and more dependent on the United States for our export trade. In the third place I had pointed' out the unfortunate position in which the United Kingdom now finds herself, by reason of which that former great customer of ours has been compelled to cut down on her purchases of goods from Canada.
One other basic fact in connection with Canada's external trade which I wish to place before the house this evening is the similar situation which prevails with regard to our trade with Australia and New Zealand. In the years before the war those two sister dominions were among our best customers. At one time Australia was our third largest customer. We now find that she has slipped away down the list until she is seventh.
I have here the annual report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1951. On page 13 thereof we find a list of Canada's leading export customers during the calendar year 1951. In first place stood the United States with purchases of $2,298 million; in second place was the United Kingdom, very much below the United States but with purchases of $631 million. In the third place we find Belgium and Luxembourg with total purchases from Canada of $94 million. In the fourth place it is surprising to find Japan with purchases of $73 million. I am wondering 
how much of that amount is accounted for by iron ore from British Columbia which is being purchased by Japan and sold back to us at a greatly increased price in the form of steel. In fifth place was Brazil with $54 million; then the Union of South Africa with $53 million; and in seventh place was Australia with only $49 million worth of purchases during 1951. Then there follow eight other nations, namely Italy, France, Germany, India, Norway, Mexico, Venezuela and The Netherlands, making a total of fifteen named altogether. New Zealand is not even in the first fifteen whereas back before the war she was at one time, I think, our fifth best customer. The trade situation between Canada and Australia and New Zealand is therefore extremely bad. That matter is, of course, of great interest to us on the Pacific coast. The figures I have given are for exports only, and I presume the figures for imports which Canada has purchased from Australia and New Zealand would show an even worse picture.
To come down to the actual problems which are facing our people in British Columbia in connection with export trade, I would point out to the house that we are being badly hurt in that province because of the reduction in trade within the commonwealth. This afternoon the leader of the opposition explained the extremely difficult position of the cheese producers in Ontario and Quebec by reason of the loss of the British market. In my province we have lost entirely our market in the United Kingdom for canned salmon; we have largely lost our market for lumber and we have lost entirely our market for apples. These are some commodities which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did not mention this afternoon. He spoke about materials in which trade has increased. I admit at once that in the strategic materials, such as metals, there has been an increase which has been brought about because those metals are required by the United Kingdom for defence preparations. But they do not give the whole picture. A conference is needed in order to meet this situation in such commodities as canned salmon, lumber and apples.
To deal first with the canned salmon, may I say that our salmon canning industry was greatly worried early this spring when it was announced in Great Britain that there would be a slash in the imports of certain commodities. Britain has been our best export market for canned salmon, and it was feared that we would lose it by reason of those cuts. In due course that was what happened. About the middle of April Britain announced that she would not buy any canned salmon from Canada during the present year. That meant the loss of a business

which ran to over $6 million per year. It was an extremely serious blow for our salmon packers and also for the men engaged in the fishing industry; in fact it was a serious blow for the whole province.
Last month the fisheries council of Canada held their annual meeting in Vancouver. They dealt with this question of the export market for canned salmon and passed a strong resolution which urged the government, just as we are urging today, that it should explore every avenue of action with a view to broadening the area of export markets available to Canadian fishery products. The resolution went on to point out that many countries still want our fish but cannot get it because of exchange obstacles. These men in the industry pointed out that the industry can try to make the price attractive, but only the government can lick the dollar-sterling problem. How true is that observation.
We find statements being made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), who is the only British Columbia representative in the cabinet. I have here a dispatch from a little publication put out by the province of British Columbia from their overseas office in London. It is dated June, this present month, and is headed "B.C. and the British Market". It refers to a statement made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) at this meeting of the fisheries council, and quotes him as follows:
"We haven't lost the British market for B.C. salmon. It has been postponed. I don't like the idea to be held that it's gone permanently. It's only been delayed because the British had to delay it. Their people are still really hungry for Canadian canned salmon."
What we object to is the government sitting back and doing nothing to remedy this situation. It was not very many days after the meeting of the fisheries council until word was received that the United Kingdom had purchased a large quantity of Russian salmon. In that deal they bought about one-third of the total amount that previously had been purchased from British Columbia. This development may mean that our market for canned salmon will be lost to Russia, if you please.
I hold in my hand a press dispatch containing a statement made by Mr. S. M. Rosenberg, who is one of our leading fishing men on the west coast to the following effect:
"It's a real disappointment when your best customer turns to another source. But the industry has known for several months that the British were unlikely to buy any this year, for the first time in many years."
The article goes on:
Recently the head of the British purchasing mission in Canada, Sir Andrew Jones, told the
Suggested Commonwealth Conference canners that buying would be postponed until some means had been found to finance it, or until the exchange picture changed as regards the value of sterling in terms of Canadian dollars.
Mr. Rosenberg is quoted as not blaming the British. He said this:
"If the British had their choice they would buy in Canada rather than Russia," said Mr. Rosenberg. "It's the old story of the currency trouble. They can't buy from us if we don't buy enough from them."
That situation should not be allowed to continue. It was dealt with by the Vancouver Province in a leading editorial on May 21, entitled "A barter deal in salmon?", and reading in part as follows:
If Agriculture Minister Jimmy Gardiner can work out a three-way barter deal in meat between Canada, Great Britain and New Zealand, why can't Ottawa do something similar to recapture the British market for canned salmon?
News that British Columbia has lost about a third of its British market for canned salmon to the Soviet states is shocking news.
Nobody blames the British. They are being forced to deal with Russia by their lack of dollars.
Whatever kind of trouble it is, it is trouble that should be fixed before it gets any worse. We are losing a lot of canned salmon business. We may lose a lot of other business. Britain wants to buy our B.C. fish, fruit, lumber, minerals and other products but she can't do as she wishes because of her dollar shortage.
The editorial ends up with this paragraph, which I think is very appropriate at this time and in this debate:
If countries bound together in friendship and mutual interests can't trade freely together and are forced to do business with a country that is regarded as a common enemy, we are in a pretty fix.
Somewhat the same situation exists in lumber. I have here an editorial from Western Business, which is a very responsible business magazine published in Vancouver. I am reading from the issue of April, 1952, dealing with the position of our lumber industry:
British Columbia's lumber industry, mainstay of the province's buoyant economy in the past 15 years, is faced with a serious deterioration of its fundamental position, its overseas markets have suddenly closed with the renewed austerity programs of the U.K. and sterling areas so that only a trickle of business is coming from these markets which took nearly 43 per cent of B.C.'s lumber production last year. Bulk buying of the past 12 years by Britain, which gave Canada an assured forward position for as much as a year on an important part of the lumber cut, is now a thing of the past. Private U.K. buyers are underfinanced to meet Britain's needs and must obtain treasury permits to expend scarce dollars for lumber. Australia has cancelled import permits for lumber. Other markets are similarly controlled so that for the first time in the history of the B.C. lumber industry there is such an un-free overseas market as to make the selling of lumber at some negotiated price virtually impossible at present.
In the next month, May, we find the same story in the annual report of B.C. Forest Products Limited, one of our large lumber

Suggested Commonwealth Conference producers. The president of that company is E. P. Taylor of Toronto, and in his annual report he described the situation as follows:
Immediate prospects are poor for selling any large volume of our products at profitable prices to our overseas buyers. It appears that this industry will have to concentrate its sales in the North American market to a greater extent than ever before. It is unlikely that a market can be found which in price and volume will replace those overseas markets now denied this industry.
Mr. Taylor said the poor prospects were due to world-wide exchange difficulties. Last of the company's large British orders will be filled during the summer.
The same situation exists with apples. We produce the finest apples in the world in the interior of British Columbia.
Do you say that with a smile?
Agreed.

One of their best markets has been the United Kingdom. In addition, they have had markets in other portions of the commonwealth. That market is now gone, and unless some steps are taken to meet this exchange and trade situation Canadians will suffer. Let us leave out of the picture for the time being the consideration of the injury done to other parts of the commonwealth. Let us stress the fact that Canadians are going to suffer because of this situation; and in these three industries, salmon canning, lumber and production of apples in my province Canadians certainly are suffering.
Efforts have been made by the trade itself, both the Canadian trade and the British trade, to meet this situation. For example, less than a month ago a group of British manufacturers set up in Vancouver what is described as an import centre. They have done that in a move to promote trade between Great Britain and the west coast of Canada. One of the British spokesmen for that movement described what they were trying to do by this import centre when he spoke in Vancouver just a short time ago. I wish to quote a few paragraphs from the statement, because it sets out the situation very clearly. He said:
Our object is intensive exploitation of the Canadian market for British goods so that the natural trade between the two countries can be restored and expanded.
The article goes on:
He hopes the plan will mean many U.K.-bound ships out of B.C. ports with grain, lumber, canned salmon, mine concentrates, aluminum ingot, beef and bacon. On return trips, these ships would unload a greatly expanded volume of British engineering goods and consumer manufactures. British importers and agents would open many new offices here; they also would establish processing and finishing plants.
Mr. Forbes goes on to say:
There is a "pent-up demand" in the U.K. for B.C. lumber for houses, salmon for the table and the
tMr. Green.]

whole range of foods that Canada once supplied. The list includes beef, pork, cheese and fish. Canada continues a major supplier of wheat.
B.C. exporters of lumber and fish, who haven't a future order on file from Britain, traditionally the big customer for these products, have their representatives at the Vancouver meeting.
That is an excellent move, and I hope it will help to meet the situation. But surely the government can do something to help solve this problem. As a preliminary step we advocate the calling of this conference of the various nations of the commonwealth. I do not believe that either the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) this afternoon gave one valid reason for not calling that conference; in fact, the impression I gained was that they were not very much worried about the whole situation, and were inclined to laugh off the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew).
I suggest to them and to the house that such a conference could do no harm, and it might be a great help. Surely it is worth while to do something to meet this situation. The meat deal, the deal made for the disposal of our beef, shows at least one thing, and that is that when a situation is tough enough some kind of remedy can be found. I am not saying that this barter deal was wise or the best move that could have been made; but the government got into the position where something had to be done, and the deal resulted.
There is just as great need to take some steps about this convertibility question, and the question of our trade with the commonwealth. I can only regret that the ministers have taken the attitude that they will have nothing whatever to do with this proposal for a conference.
You know, sometimes we do not take advantage of our position in the commonwealth. We do not go after the benefits we could get if we were a little more aggressive. I should like to close my remarks by quoting a statement made by the president of the board of trade in the United Kingdom last month. Dealing with the possibilities for trade within the commonwealth, and speaking on the eve of the commonwealth trade day at the British industries fair, he said:
What is important for us is to share a common aim and that aim should be the development of our resources and the expansion of our trade. That is not a narrow selfish policy. I firmly believe that by developing the commonwealth we shall increase the trade we do with other nations, and thereby enrich the world.
All we are asking is that the government of Canada adopt a policy at the present time with that same objective in mind.

Mr. Speaker, Kipling has said that-
East is east, and west is west,
And never the twain shall meet.
That certainly is not true of this debate. We have just heard the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) speak in support of the amendment and point out the full importance of the matters envisaged in the amendment to his own province on the Pacific coast. I say, sir, that those matters are of equal importance to those of us in eastern Canada. In fact I believe I can say they are of even greater importance than on the Pacific coast, if that is possible.
In the first place the markets across the ocean, the markets in Great Britain, have been traditionally those of the maritime provinces and eastern Canada. We were servicing those markets in the days of wooden ships, when the flag of the province of Nova Scotia was seen on the seven seas, and when we had hundreds of ships under sail. Although those ships covered all the markets of the world, primarily they were engaged in an export trade to the markets of Great Britain; and that condition existed even before there was a central Canadian or western Canadian market.
Then, in addition to the tradition, there is the matter of our geographical position. The cost of transport by rail freight from eastern Canadian points to central Canada makes it more difficult for us to enjoy the Canadian market. And in the third place, of course our natural position, jutting out as we do like a wharf into the north Atlantic, and with relatively cheap water rates, has given an impetus to the establishment of markets in Great Britain and the rest of Europe, but principally in Great Britain.
We in the east today are facing a serious situation-as, of course, are all Canadians. But I suggest that we are suffering from an even more serious difficulty because of the threatened or actual loss of those markets brought about by a diminution or disappearance of sterling in sufficient quantities.
I have of course a particular interest in the way these problems affect my own constituency, because we are almost entirely dependent upon the export market of Great Britain for the support of our apple industry. Before the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra leaves the chamber I would point out that the apple industry in my part of the country is the oldest and, may I add, the best in Canada. It was developed and we were shipping apples to Britain more than half a century ago. That condition continued down through the years until recently, when it has been threatened.
Suggested Commonwealth Conference I can remember the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when speaking in the house a year ago, shrugging off the problem of the British market by saying that Great Britain was no longer importing Canadian apples, and no longer offered a market for our apples-period. His bald statement was that Britain was producing sufficient apples of her own and did not wish to import any.
That was an utterly ridiculous statement and I feel sure the right hon. gentleman must have known it, because last year Great Britain imported over 4 million hundredweight of apples of which Canada supplied less than 13 per cent. Yet in 1946 we supplied 69 per cent of the entire British market; and in 1938, before the war, we were supplying virtually 50 per cent of the entire British market.
Last year, as I say, that was reduced to 13 per cent, and the intimation is that the British government has said that this year there will be no sterling available for the purchase of apples. This is of importance to us in the east, and as was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra it is also important to the apple industry in his province. Let me add that it is also of tremendous importance to the apple industry of Ontario and Quebec; make no mistake about that. If the Canadian exporters in British Columbia and Nova Scotia are denied export markets because of a lack of sterling, then there will be a dislocation of the Canadian market which will be most serious indeed.
That was one reason-I think it was the primary reason-why during the war this government did assist the fruit growing industry of Nova Scotia, and to some extent of British Columbia, so as to preserve orderly marketing in central Canada. So this matter is of far more than provincial importance; it is a matter affecting all of Canada, and in so far as that particular industry is concerned, goes to the very root of it. If the apple industry of this dominion is to be preserved and is to continue, then you have to solve the sterling problem. If you do not solve it the apple industry will suffer a disaster from which it will take many years to recover.
It is not only the apple industry in the maritime provinces that is concerned. For many years we have exported lumber and pit props from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to Great Britain, but we are now threatened with a loss of that market. The lumber dealers in both provinces are worried about this matter. I think some of that worry was reflected in the events of last Monday in New Brunswick, because certainly it was in part the anxiety over these lost
