Suggested Commonwealth Conference markets and this problem of sterling which I found, and which I am sure others found, reflected in the minds of the people with whom I discussed matters prior to the byelections which took place a week ago yesterday.
In addition to markets for lumber, in Nova Scotia we also have our salt fish and cured fish industries which were dependent upon export markets, not so much in Great Britain but in the West Indies. Again because of this loss of sterling and because of the particular problems in those islands we are faced with the loss of further markets. We have had hopes of attracting to the maritime provinces, because of our geographical position, industries based upon export markets. We believe we have opportunities for that type of industry, but basic export trade is dependent upon the markets of Great Britain and the commonwealth. Until this sterling problem is solved we will have little hope of attracting such industries.
For these reasons and many others which could be enumerated I repeat that this problem of sterling is of tremendous importance to the east. Both ministers who spoke this afternoon suggested that there was nothing that could be done about it. One of them said we had not received an invitation to any conference to deal with this matter. Why wait for an invitation? This is the problem which goes to the very root of our economic existence in this country. I suggest that the government should be giving a lead in this matter rather than waiting for an invitation.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pointed out a few minutes ago,
I am quite sure if we on this side of the house had suggested six weeks ago that a barter deal might be arranged among the United States, Great Britain and Canada, we would have been laughed at by hon. gentlemen on the other side. They would have told us that it was impossible to conceive of such a thing. Yet when the necessity arose it did mot take long to work out such a deal. I remember reading not long ago- this is perhaps not apropos of this matter- where the Prime Minister of Great Britain, confronted with a problem, made a barter deal to use Malaya tin and aluminum which he had under contract from Canada to obtain steel from the United States. It seems that when there is a will there is a way in which these things can be accomplished. We can and should be able to find a way.
I might suggest one minor way. If we were selling products in Great Britain some of the sterling in payment thereof could be allocated for the purchase of products from

Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry to have to take part in this debate, because I do not think it should be going on at all. I will reassure the minister that I am not going to be long. The reason I do not think it should be going on has already been stated. No reason has been given against the desirability of adopting this amendment except the reason which none of us is going to accept and which I am sure the minister did not really want the house to accept, that nothing can be done. The amendment reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies-
I do not imagine anyone is going to deny that that is a desirable thing. The amendment continues:
-and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
I do not think anyone will deny that that is a good thing. After all, for generations trade across the north Atlantic has been our lifeblood.
One of the points I wish to make is that you cannot do anything until you believe it really needs to be done. One of the things that bothers me is that we are faced with an extraordinary degree of self-satisfaction on the part of the government. Why that should be so strong I do not know. When we asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) about trade with the United Kingdom he said, "Don't worry about it, I made a speech in the Guildhall." I have no doubt that it was an adequate speech, but that does not seem to me to be an adequate answer to the question. On May 15 the minister expressed his views about trade in rather glowing terms, and I quote from page 2240 of Hansard as follows:
Instead of losing markets we are shipping more to the markets we are supposed to be losing. As I say, we have markets for everything that Canada can produce. We have been able to find the very best markets in the world, and as a result the Canadian economy is at the highest point of prosperity it has ever reached in the history of the country.
That makes strange reading in the light of what we have listened to from the hon. mem-oer for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). We have heard of lost markets for lumber, apples and salmon in the west and for apples, fish and other things in the east.
Suggested Commonwealth Conference For the minister to tell us that markets have been found for everything just does not make sense. The truth of the matter is that the minister has his mind-and I think he is constituted this way-concentrated, and very properly so, on the work he is doing, which I think is good. He has just one interest and will not admit that there is anything that is not good or anything with which he has not dealt.
Another thing that bothers me is that, for a man who is practical in so many ways, he will insist on this foolish habit of talking constantly about dollars and answering complaints that trade is being lost by saying that we are shipping far more than we were years ago and always giving the result in dollars. He ought to know better than anyone else how much dollars have been depreciated, in large measure by the policies of his own government, in the last few years; and he should not fob us off with that sort of thing again.
The other point I wish: to make is that we are of course in the midst of a boom. Booms are often mysterious things. They sometimes come without anyone being able to say how they came and they certainly go without anyone being quite sure how they have gone. But there need be no mystery about this boom. It was caused by defence preparation. We all understand how it came, and when the minister tells us about the fine state of our trade, as he did this afternoon, he entirely omits one very important thing. He should have been explaining to us that our exports to a very large extent-I shall not attempt to put it into figures-are due to the entirely accidental fact that we are preparing at the present time for war.
One of two things will happen. Either war will come, which we all pray will not happen, in which case all calculations will be thrown into the discard. If war does not come, then may I point out that the minister has been the first person to tell us that our defence preparations are bound to slow down because the pipe lines will be filled up. Therefore when we consider the situation at the moment we are just like men sleepwalking. We are just like men who will not look at the facts if we are not prepared to realize that a situation which we all hope is temporary and which we all hope is going to come to an end may do so, and that if it does come to an end or slackens in any way it will alter the whole situation.
Can any of us imagine what it would be like if by some magic which we cannot foresee the apprehension of war should pass away? Any number of the markets where
2878	HOUSE OF
Suggested Commonwealth Conference we are now selling would disappear. Therefore I say we should be taking these things into account. If that situation happened we would suddenly find that our markets for wheat, metals and lumber had been transformed beyond our worst dreams. The problem is whether it is worth while to make the effort. The ministers say we are making efforts and there is nothing more to be done. They say we have not been asked to a trade conference. I think that last reason is a trivial one. This government is not usually so modest when it has a view to express. Actually we have fallen into the habit, which I believe is a very bad one, of thinking that the currency problems of northern Europe and the sterling area is their problem and not ours. The truth of the matter is that it is just as much ours as theirs. We all remember the word used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) some years ago after returning from- an imperial conference at Colombo. He came back and said that he had exercised the functions of a gadfly. I am not very familiar with gadflies but I understand their function is purely that of stinging. Apparently he conceived his function at that conference to be to stir up other people, presumably to be more active and alert in their own interests.
I think that is an entire misunderstanding. I noticed when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) attended such a conference last January his position was described as something in the nature of a benevolent observer. I am not sure of those two words but that was the general tenor. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is more realistic. He really thinks we need to sell the farm products we raise, and he is a little impatient with financial difficulties. The financial difficulties are real enough and they cannot be dispelled just by a wave of the hand. We all know that, and I think it would be well for us to remember it. I thought of it particularly this afternoon when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was giving us the extraordinary disparity in prices. I think we had better ask ourselves whether we are creating for ourselves in North America a position of isolation which, however splendid it may look now, may not always look so splendid if we get to the position where we have a scale of prices and of costs which cuts us off from other markets.
Therefore I say this is not a problem of somebody else. It is a problem we are terribly interested in ourselves. As I said a moment ago, when the smoke clears away and if, as we all hope, we reach the stage where feverish preparations for war come


to an end, then we will suddenly be faced with the question of markets. We will suddenly be faced with the realization that the sterling area, particularly northern Europe, has been our haven in years past. We may also be faced with the sudden realization of the fact that the United States is in very many ways a competitor rather than a market.
It seems to me the first thing for us to do is believe that this serious problem is our problem. It has already been stated that when you really want to do a thing there are ways to do it. I quoted a music hall catch in the house the other night to the effect that where there is a will there are three ways.
I should like to say a word about convertibility. As I said a moment ago, nobody has suggested that convertibility is easy. I have here The Economist of May 24 of this year, which contains a reference to a meeting of the International Chamber of Commerce at which the question of convertibility was discussed. I am not going to read from the article because the things they have to say are not new. They talk about the need to free exchanges and they suggest various things, the responsibility of the creditor countries, the responsibility of the international monetary fund and so on. I am not going to go into that. I am merely going to say that I cannot see why anyone should doubt that it is a good thing for us to meet together to discuss, again and again if you wish, this problem.
We ought to have something to contribute. We ought to know something about the value of free exchange. We certainly made enough mistakes ourselves. First of all we overvalued our dollar to the extent that in 1947 we lost about a billion dollars in United States funds. Then later we undervalued it. Therefore we ought to have experience to contribute. I do not think any evidence could be better than ours. I suggest the amendment is a sensible one, that it might very well be acted upon, and that not to do so is really just another instance of that unregenerate political pride of the government to which we are so accustomed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the amendment because I think it will go a long way towards solving the problems of the dairy farmers in my constituency and elsewhere in the province of Ontario. Anyone who has studied our export trade since the end of the first great war knows that our national income varies directly with our export trade. If our exports are up in any one year, then our national income follows in almost exactly the same proportion in the following year. And if our exports are down in a year, then our national income can be counted on to follow suit in almost the same proportion in the following year. Therefore the phrase "export or die" applies particularly to our Canadian economy.
During the past few months most of the commonwealth countries have been forced to drastically curtail their imports in order to save dollars. If we are to continue to do business with these countries we must take their products in payment for our exports. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that, as the only non-sterling country in the British commonwealth of nations, we should take the initiative in calling a commonwealth trade conference. Through this medium trade experts from Canada could sit down with experts from other commonwealth countries


and work out the means of expanding our trade, rather than simply taking the negative course of restricting imports in the hope that something will eventually fall into our laps.
I believe this government owes it to the primary and secondary producers of this country at least to make an attempt to retain our traditional markets until the convertibility of sterling again becomes a reality.
This government says the kind of conference I have mentioned is unnecessary, and they point to the favourable position of our gold and dollar reserves. Anybody will agree that this position is very good today. But it is not good because of a favourable balance of trade, but because of the very heavy inflow of capital into this country for development purposes. Much as this capital inflow is welcome to Canada, no reasonably minded person expects that it will continue indefinitely; and if we are to maintain our favourable position with regard to our international stability, then we must bend every effort to build up our export markets.

Look at the number of outlets we have in the United States"; because the history of our trade with the United States has made us realize that this market is very uncertain, and it has in no way the stability of the markets we have enjoyed in the United Kingdom.
This of course is readily understandable because of the similarity of their production to ours. I believe the only long-term solution to this problem is a greater willingness and ability to exchange products within the British commonwealth of nations. I believe the only way this can be worked out is by our sitting down with other members of the British commonwealth, talking the matter over and deciding what products of ours they can take in return for our being willing to take certain products of theirs. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I very sincerely urge this government to take the initiative in calling a British commonwealth trade conference at the very earliest opportunity.

What do we find today? The market for each one of these products has almost disappeared.
It disappeared in 1929.

AH we are saying to the government now is that when they are repeating the same episode again, when they are riding the gravy train of war prosperity, they should stop and take one look at the situation and call a trade conference, not a conference of finance ministers but a conference of trade departments where the experts would be in attendance. It is not good enough to have an exhibition in Toronto. It is not good enough to build big machines and look at them. You should have a British commonwealth trade conference as we had in 1932.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What you need is cash, Earl.

Yes. I notice the Minister of Finance is very interested in cash. No one handles more of it more recklessly than he does, but that is not good enough. I know


you need cash, and evidently there is a lot of it in your department. You have taken more than 50 per cent of everybody's cash in this dominion, and you will take more. The only hope we have for tax relief is an election in 1953. When next year's budget is presented I think Canada will know almost when the election will take place.
The matter goes further. I say in all sincerity I do not believe there is an hon. member within the sound of my voice, no matter to what party he belongs and irrespective of race, class or creed, who does not believe in his heart of hearts that the very nucleus of the United Nations is the British commonwealth of nations. It is the heart, it is the soul of the United Nations in international affairs. It is the beacon light and the force that has given inspiration. My hon. friends may laugh but in their innermost private thinking I know they agree that it is the inspiring force that brought the United Nations together. Without a strong British commonwealth of nations there is very little hope for world affairs in the future, and the only way to strengthen it is by trade.
We are a member of the British commonwealth. We are the senior dominion. It is our duty not to attend a conference called by some minor or junior member of the commonwealth but as the senior dominion of the British commonwealth to propose a conference, sit down and see what can be done and report back. It may be that nothing can be done, but if that is the case we will accept that because you have attended scores of conferences in the past where you did nothing. There is as much hope for the success of the conference we suggest as there was for the success of many others.
You have spent millions of the people's money travelling all over the world to conferences. You are the greatest travellers this country has seen since confederation. I ask you to take one more trip. You are getting old and weary, and it will probably be your last. Take one more trip to look into the possibilities of a British trade conference and see if you cannot restore the trade that you have lost for the second time in a quarter of a century. I have mentioned only a few of the things lost, particularly those having to do with agriculture. I know the farmers of Canada realize quite well that we are better off to depend on a stable British market than on the market in the United States, even though in time of war they will pay us big prices. I can well recall that in 1922 we thought we had a market for beef cattle in the United States. When the slump came in that country that market was cut off overnight. First there was the Fordney-McCumber tariff. Then

there was the Hawley-Smoot tariff. Recently restrictions were imposed on our dairy products. We have lost the cheese market in Great Britain. We have lost the bacon and apple markets in Great Britain. He is an optimist who says that in normal times you can recover what has been lost by selling to the United States. I am not going to go further except to say that, independent of politics, I urge the government to reconsider the proposal to call a British commonwealth trade conference in order to find out if something cannot be done with respect to the convertibility of exchange and the recovery of markets that have been lost.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Surely.
I understand the hon. member, whom I greatly admire-
Thank you.
-to suggest that he should have one more trip. Would he advocate that it be to the Hambletonian races at Goshen?
Mr. Speaker, I would not mind that, and I might get one for the hon. member if he wants to go. I think probably he is in better shape for it than I would be.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Question?
Mr. Speaker, it is hardly worth while voting tonight.
It is hardly worth voting, period.

Most of us have sat here all day and listened to some good speeches, and some that were not so good. The question is too serious, in my opinion, to just allow a certain number of members from a certain group to get up and make a lot of speeches without very much substance behind them.
Hear, hear.

We all know the international marketing question is a difficult one, and there is no tailor-made formula whereby you are going to work it out. I think it is sufficiently serious that if the Conservative party had a policy and a program they thought could iron out the international difficulties in marketing which are world-wide now, I would like to see that formula laid on the table.
It is quite all right to call a conference, and we are agreeable that a conference should be called. It might be helpful to get the sterling countries around a table with the dollar countries and see what might be done. But we have had a lot of conferences. We had the Bretton Woods conference, and we 55704-182
Suggested Commonwealth Conference sent the best financial brains this country had to it. Britain had her representatives there, as had all our allies. We had just finished a war, a war that was largely the result of the collapse of the economic system on a world scale. All these best brains went to the Bretton Woods conference and they decided that an international bank was necessary. That international bank had as one of its functions preventing the depreciation of currencies. A lot of mechanisms that were useful and perhaps would have been workable were suggested. A lot of people put a lot of monkey wrenches in that machinery, and Britain was practically driven away from it.
I had not intended to take time in this debate at all providing the opposition had been willing to take a vote around 10.30 p.m. but frankly, as far as I am concerned, the hon. gentleman has for today talked out his own motion. In all his discussions, the only solution he had was to give the Conservative party power. That swan song was sung by Mr. Churchill very recently. Another government was in power, a government that was bringing new mechanics to bear on the changing structure of society. Whether you like it or not it has changed. Mr. Churchill took power, and he was going to solve the problems of Britain overnight. He is not solving them; and mind you, I am not crabbing about that because I knew, as well as the hon. gentleman who just took his seat knows, that in the situation which faced Mr. Churchill when he formed a government he was not going to be able to solve those problems overnight. He is gradually whittling his way back to where he was in 1939.
Just giving the Conservative party power in the present circumstances is not going to solve the international marketing question. As the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) says, that might put us back to 1930. There is one thing of which I am convinced. As far as the old scheme of things is concerned, it went out when the shooting started in the last war. We are embarked in a world where there are not very many mileposts and the old methods of marketing as between country and country are gone.
The reason we are losing the British market is very obvious. Depreciation of her currency is in part responsible. Also the other countries of Europe, including Russia, are willing to do barter trade with Great Britain. This group has proposed on several occasions in this house-and we have moved amendments in connection with the matter of apples as pertaining to Nova Scotia, and the matter of salmon in western Canada-that for particular commodities we should arrange an exchange with Britain. My hon. friends at that time were very solidly opposed. As far
2888	HOUSE OF
Suggested Commonwealth Conference as we are concerned we believe, and have done so for a long time, that the only successful way of conducting international trade is by an exchange of goods. Otherwise you give away the real wealth of your country for paper.
Unless the government that is in power in this country decides on a change in the mechanism of international marketing within the next few years, and gets away from money as a medium of exchange, in my opinion you are going to have just what you have now. Mr. Churchill is finding out. I know that he does not like barter, but he is willing to barter machinery for wheat with soviet Russia.
Seventy-five per cent of all the old methods of international trade have gone out. A large percentage of the people of the world with whom we are going to try to trade are operating on socialist mechanisms in international trade. Whether you like that word is immaterial. What most people are afraid of is the interpretation that other people have built up.
The whole structure of society has changed. It is not going to be as simple as my hon. friend thinks; that all you have to do is get up and make a political speech saying that the government has done this or has not done that, when there are no facts behind that kind of speech.
In the matter of changing governments, if you are going to make any change, if your socks are dirty you generally put on a cleaner pair.

At least you wash
them.

Yes, wash them or put on a cleaner pair. In this matter of free enterprise, whether it is in the domestic field or in the international field, the party that seeks to take power from the present government has exactly the same policy. They do not intend

to change anything, but to just go on and on and on. It is a matter of "we are in and you are out".
Eleven o'clock.

I am not prepared to accept from anyone in this house the statement that we are going to solve the problem by the Conservative party taking power. We want to have better information than the people of Britain got from Mr. Churchill about what another government would do. The fact of the matter is that he is not doing so well, and that was pretty clearly indicated by the swing in the council elections in Britain. The trend is away.

Eleven o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Gillis the debate was adjourned.
